CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: China should maintain its retaliatory posture and signal willingness to negotiate from a position of strength, but avoid further unilateral escalation beyond matching U.S. moves. We should continue diversifying trade partners and lowering tariffs on non-U.S. goods to reduce dependency.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high but not yet existential. As of November 2018, the U.S. has imposed tariffs on $250 billion of Chinese imports (roughly half of bilateral trade), with Trump threatening to tariff the remaining $267 billion if China retaliates (Fox Business/Motley Fool transcript). China has retaliated on $110 billion of $130 billion in U.S. imports it receives, covering nearly all bilateral trade (Fox Business). Soybean prices have fallen 20% affecting U.S. farmers, but China's export economy—particularly technology assembly and manufacturing—faces significant disruption. The Brookings analysis notes that while China is the final assembler, more than half the value of products like smartphones comes from parts made in South Korea and Japan, meaning U.S. tariffs on Chinese exports damage global value chains and create collateral damage for U.S. firms operating in China. However, China's retaliatory capacity is constrained: it imports only $130 billion of U.S. goods versus $506 billion the U.S. imports from China, meaning China cannot match tariff-for-tariff (CBS News). The Washington Post reports that Chinese leaders feel betrayed after multiple failed deal attempts with Ross and Mnuchin that Trump personally vetoed, suggesting the U.S. negotiating position is unreliable. China has strategically lowered tariffs on goods from other countries to redirect its consumers away from U.S. products (Fox Business). The threat score of +0.55 reflects that major export sectors are under tariff pressure, nearly all bilateral trade is now tariffed, and there is risk of further escalation to cover 100% of trade. The action score of -1 (retaliate) reflects that China has already matched U.S. moves and should continue to do so to maintain leverage, while signaling openness to talks after the U.S. midterm elections as Brookings suggests is the likely window for negotiation.
key_factors: U.S. tariffs now cover $250 billion of Chinese imports (~50% of bilateral trade), with threat to tariff remaining $267 billion
China has retaliated on $110B of $130B in U.S. imports, nearly exhausting retaliatory capacity
China's asymmetric trade position ($506B U.S. imports from China vs $130B China imports from U.S.) limits matching ability
Multiple failed U.S.-China deal attempts (Ross deal, Mnuchin deal) vetoed by Trump suggest unreliable negotiating partner
China strategically lowering tariffs on non-U.S. goods to redirect supply chains away from American products
Global value chain disruption: China as final assembler but >50% value from other countries (Japan, South Korea)
U.S. midterm elections just concluded (Nov 6, 2018) creating potential window for renewed negotiations

China also announced some tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods... This second round of Chinese tariffs is going to now cover $110 billion of the $130 billion of U.S.-China trade -- again, almost 100% of the entire trading relationship
China has promised to respond in kind, but it would be unable to match that amount since it imported only $130 billion of U.S. goods last year

While China is the final assembler from many products, actually more than half of the value of those products are in parts and components from other countries like South Korea and Japan

while they've increased the tariffs on American goods, they've lowered the tariffs on some of the other goods from other places... That's an effort to try to drive their own consumers away from choosing U.S. products and choosing others
